newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen prepares for first vote since civil war.
newsitem.headline: Yemen prepares for first vote since civil war.

text.p: Candidates began signing up on Thursday for Yemen's first general election since a civil war in 1994 nearly tore apart the Middle East's poorest country.
Election officials expect about 5,000 candidates to seek votes for 301 parliamentary seats under the banners of 12 parties or as independents in the April 27 election.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), some of whose former leaders launched the southern separatist campaign that sparked the war, and two others have announced they will boycott the poll because of alleged irregularities.
Some 4.6 million of the 7.5 million people aged 18 and over who are eligible to vote out of a population of 16 million had registered to vote when the process ended last August.
The YSP won 50 seats in the outgoing assembly, dominated by the General People's Congress (GPC) of President Ali Abdullah Saleh and its junior coalition partner the Islamist Islah Party.

Western diplomats expect the GPC to return as the governing party and then move further to meet World Bank demands for economic reforms. Observers from the European Union, the United States and Eastern Europe will monitor the election.
An impoverished and fractious republic with a vigorous but fragmented opposition, Yemen is a small independent oil producer nestling on the southern border of Saudi Arabia.
"This is a fledgling democracy surrounded by inward-looking countries disturbed by democracy on their doorstep," a Western diplomat told Reuters.
"The election is flawed -- 80,000 cases of double entries in voter registration -- but they are getting there."

In recent years the country's fragile unity has been plagued by internal conflict. Kidnappings -- seven German tourists were held for more than a week earlier this month -- are occasionally carried out by tribesmen with grievances, usually over property.

The Yemeni republic was founded in September 1962 when officers toppled a religious monarchy that had lasted 1,000 years. The 1990 merger of the once royalist north and the Marxist south ended hundreds of years of separation.

In 1994 a southern separatist bid followed a crisis between Saleh and Ali Salem al-Baidh, YSP leader and his deputy. In the civil war that ensued forces loyal to the president crushed the secessionists.

"It takes time to heal. The civil war was an inside thing, within a family. You even found brothers on opposing sides killing each other," deputy information minister Amat al-Aleem Ali Alsoswa told Reuters.
"Yemen is not homogeneous. It is very different. A democracy would hold it together, but more is needed. It is the only way to marginalise our differences."

Tarek al-Shami, spokesman for an eight-party opposition cordinating group, said some opposition parties had set a condition of national reconciliation and amnesty for 15 exiled YSP leaders accused of starting the war.
But not all eight parties agreed with the boycott.
"We cannot say our democracy is the best or is a model democracy. But we are taking the first steps," Shami said.
The first substantive session of the trial in absentia of the 15 leading secessionists was held in Sanaa last Saturday and adjourned until May 10.
Saleh, a former artillery officer born in 1942, was re-elected to a second four-year term by parliamentary deputies on October 1, 1994. His job is not in contention next month.
